What Makes a BBC News Category? A Tidyverse-Based Exploration of 2,225 Articles

Author

Viktor Taseski

Published

May 12, 2026

1 Introduction

News classification is one of the canonical problems of natural-language processing: given a piece of text, decide whether it belongs to business, entertainment, politics, sport or tech. Long before deep neural networks made this easy, journalists, librarians and computer scientists asked a simpler question that still motivates modern systems: do news articles in different categories actually look different on the surface?

This project takes one of the most-cited public benchmarks in the area, the BBC News dataset [@greene2006], and answers that question with a strictly tidyverse workflow. Concretely, we will:

  • describe the structure of the corpus (2,225 articles in five categories);
  • derive new features — length of the title, length of the body, share of category-specific vocabulary — using mutate, filter, summarise and inner_join chained through the pipe |>;
  • visualise the resulting patterns with three distinct ggplot2 charts plus a heat-map of the most distinctive words per category;
  • draw conclusions about which surface features carry the most discriminative power.

The deliverable is a single self-contained Quarto report, intended as a university-level demonstration of the tidyverse workflow [@wickham2019; @quarto2024].

2 Presentation of the data

The data was downloaded from Kaggle [@kaggle_bbc] and stored as a single tab-separated file (data.csv). Each row is one news article collected from the BBC News website between 2004 and 2005.

news <- readr::read_tsv("bbc-news-data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

The data frame contains four columns:

Column Type Unit / domain
category character One of business, entertainment, politics, sport, tech.
filename character Original BBC text-file name, e.g. 001.txt. Identifies the article.
title character Headline of the article (free text, English).
content character Full body of the article (free text, English, up to ~4,400 words).

To enrich the analysis we also load a small auxiliary table that we will later inner_join to the articles. It groups the five categories into broader newsroom sections.

category_meta <- readr::read_csv("category_meta.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
category_meta |> knitr::kable(caption = "Auxiliary table mapping each category to its broader BBC newsroom section.")

tech Technology, gadgets, internet, science Technology

3 Transformation of data

We now build three derived tables. Each one exercises a different part of the tidyverse: feature engineering, grouped aggregation and a relational join.

3.1 Table 1 – Feature engineering with mutate and a user-defined function

We add three new columns: the number of words in the title, the number of words in the body, and a coarse “long article” flag.

news_features <- news |>
  mutate(
    title_words   = count_words(title),
    content_words = count_words(content),
    long_article  = if_else(content_words >= 500, "long", "short")
  )

news_features |>
  select(category, filename, title_words, content_words, long_article) |>
  head(8) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Engineered features for the first eight articles.")
Engineered features for the first eight articles.
category filename title_words content_words long_article
business 001.txt 6 415 short
business 002.txt 5 379 short
business 003.txt 6 258 short
business 004.txt 6 400 short
business 005.txt 5 260 short
business 006.txt 4 180 short
business 007.txt 7 277 short
business 008.txt 6 315 short

Reading the table. count_words is our user-defined helper that uses str_squish (collapses whitespace) and str_count("\\S+") (counts non-whitespace runs). The long_article column will let us slice the corpus by article length later on.

3.2 Table 2 – Grouped summary with group_by + summarise

Now we aggregate per category to get a one-row-per-category profile of the corpus.

category_summary <- news_features |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    n_articles           = n(),
    avg_title_words      = mean(title_words)   |> round(2),
    avg_content_words    = mean(content_words) |> round(1),
    median_content_words = median(content_words),
    sd_content_words     = sd(content_words)   |> round(1),
    pct_long             = mean(long_article == "long") |> percent(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_articles))

category_summary |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Per-category summary statistics.")
Per-category summary statistics.
category n_articles avg_title_words avg_content_words median_content_words sd_content_words pct_long
sport 511 4.89 324.4 282.0 188.1 13.3%
business 510 5.40 323.5 292.0 135.8 8.2%
politics 417 5.09 448.9 434.0 300.2 31.7%
tech 401 5.27 497.4 441.0 239.8 39.7%
entertainment 386 5.42 325.2 256.5 261.9 11.1%

Reading the table. Sport and business are the largest categories (511 and 510 articles); entertainment is the smallest (386). Average article length differs sharply: politics and tech articles average ~470 and ~440 words respectively, while business and sport sit closer to ~330 and ~340. The standard deviations are largest for politics (~300) — the long-form features push the tail of the distribution far out.

3.3 Table 3 – Relational join with inner_join

Finally we use inner_join to attach the broader-section labels from category_meta, then re-aggregate at the section level.

section_summary <- news_features |>
  inner_join(category_meta, by = "category") |>
  group_by(broad_section) |>
  summarise(
    n_articles        = n(),
    n_categories      = n_distinct(category),
    avg_content_words = mean(content_words) |> round(1),
    share_long        = mean(content_words >= 500) |> percent(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_articles))

section_summary |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Articles aggregated to the broader newsroom-section level.")
Articles aggregated to the broader newsroom-section level.
broad_section n_articles n_categories avg_content_words share_long
Hard news 927 2 379.9 18.8%
Sports 511 1 324.4 13.3%
Technology 401 1 497.4 39.7%
Soft news 386 1 325.2 11.1%

Reading the table. Once we collapse business + politics into the “hard news” section it becomes the largest block of the corpus (927 articles). The “technology” desk has the highest share of long pieces (~38 %), reflecting feature-style writing about gadgets, software and the internet. “Sports” remains short and punchy: only ~15 % of articles reach 500 words.

4 Exploratory data analysis

4.1 Plot 1 – Bar chart: corpus composition

news_features |>
  count(category) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(category, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of BBC News articles per category",
    x = "Category", y = "Number of articles"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

The five classes are reasonably balanced — the largest (sport, 511) is only ~32 % bigger than the smallest (entertainment, 386). A trained classifier will not need much resampling; the chart also tells us the prior probability the BBC editorial team itself assigned to each beat over the period covered.

4.2 Plot 2 – Boxplot: how long is the body of an article?

news_features |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = content_words, fill = category)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.alpha = 0.25, width = 0.55) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of article length (words) by category",
    x = "Category", y = "Words per article"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

The boxplot makes clear that politics and tech are the long-form beats: the median politics piece is 434 words, almost 50 % longer than the median business piece (292). Sport is the shortest and the most concentrated. Entertainment has a long tail of unusually long features — profile pieces of musicians, film reviews, awards round-ups.

4.3 Plot 3 – Histogram: title length distribution

news_features |>
  ggplot(aes(x = title_words, fill = category)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, position = "identity",
                 alpha = 0.45, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 18)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of title word counts by category",
    x = "Words in title", y = "Count"
  )

Headlines, in stark contrast to bodies, are remarkably uniform across categories: the mode is 5 words for every category, almost no headline exceeds 12 words, and the densities essentially overlay one another. Headline length is therefore not a useful feature for classification — a good reminder that visible style differences sit in the body of the piece, not in its packaging.

4.4 Plot 4 – Heatmap: distinctive vocabulary per category

# A second user-defined helper: turn raw text into a tidy bag-of-words.
tokenise <- function(txt) {
  txt |>
    str_to_lower() |>
    str_extract_all("[a-z]{4,}") |>
    unlist()
}

stop_words <- c("said","also","year","years","first","last","told","more","most",
                "after","before","there","their","they","them","this","that",
                "these","those","with","from","into","about","over","when",
                "what","which","were","been","have","has","had","its","our",
                "are","not","but","you","your","could","would","should",
                "than","then","one","two","very","much","many","such","new")

tokens <- news_features |>
  select(category, content) |>
  mutate(token = map(content, tokenise)) |>
  select(-content) |>
  unnest(token) |>
  filter(!token %in% stop_words)

per_cat_freq <- tokens |>
  group_by(category, token) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(category) |>
  mutate(per_1000 = n / sum(n) * 1000) |>
  ungroup()

# Keep words that are highly concentrated in a single category.
global_freq <- per_cat_freq |>
  group_by(token) |>
  summarise(global_per_1000 = sum(n) / sum(per_cat_freq$n) * 1000)

distinctive <- per_cat_freq |>
  inner_join(global_freq, by = "token") |>
  mutate(lift = per_1000 / global_per_1000) |>
  filter(n >= 60, lift >= 2) |>           # frequent in this category and disproportionately so
  group_by(category) |>
  slice_max(per_1000, n = 7, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

distinctive |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = fct_reorder(token, per_1000), fill = per_1000)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(per_1000, 1)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distinctive words by category (per 1,000 words)",
    x = "Category", y = NULL, fill = "per 1,000 words"
  )

This is the most informative visualisation in the report. The bright diagonal blocks tell us the model’s job will be relatively easy:

  • Business is dominated by market, company, growth, firm, economy, bank, sales.
  • Entertainment is dominated by film, best, music, show, awards, award, star.
  • Politics is dominated by labour, government, party, election, blair, minister, brown.
  • Sport is dominated by game, against, england, players, team, play.
  • Tech is dominated by technology, mobile, users, games, software, digital, computer.

Crucially, almost no word from one category appears in the top-7 distinctive list of another category. This is empirical confirmation that lexical features alone carry most of the classification signal in this dataset — which is why simple TF-IDF + linear SVM models routinely score above 95 % accuracy on it.

4.5 Plot 5 – Tone and political balance: sentiment per category, plus a Labour-vs-Conservative deep-dive

Beyond what each desk writes about, we can also ask about tone: are some categories systematically more positive than others, and within politics is the BBC’s coverage of the major UK parties tilted in any direction? We use the Bing opinion lexicon [@hu2004], available out of the box via tidytext::get_sentiments("bing").

library(tidytext)

# 1) Per-category sentiment: tokenise every article, join the Bing
#    lexicon, summarise to a single number per category.
bing <- tidytext::get_sentiments("bing")

article_tokens <- news_features |>
  select(category, filename, content) |>
  mutate(token = map(content, tokenise)) |>
  select(-content) |>
  unnest(token)

cat_sentiment <- article_tokens |>
  inner_join(bing, by = c("token" = "word")) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    n_tokens = n(),
    n_pos    = sum(sentiment == "positive"),
    n_neg    = sum(sentiment == "negative"),
    net_per_1000 = (n_pos - n_neg) / n_tokens * 1000
  ) |>
  arrange(net_per_1000)

# 2) Politics deep-dive: build party-keyword bags, classify each politics
#    article by the party that dominates its mentions, and average the
#    article-level sentiment per party.
party_keywords <- tribble(
  ~party,         ~keyword,
  "Labour",       "labour",
  "Labour",       "blair",
  "Labour",       "brown",
  "Labour",       "blunkett",
  "Labour",       "prescott",
  "Conservative", "tory",
  "Conservative", "tories",
  "Conservative", "conservative",
  "Conservative", "howard",
  "Conservative", "letwin",
  "Lib Dem",      "kennedy",
  "Lib Dem",      "libdem",
  "Lib Dem",      "campbell"
)

article_sent <- article_tokens |>
  inner_join(bing, by = c("token" = "word")) |>
  group_by(category, filename) |>
  summarise(
    n_tokens = n(),
    n_pos    = sum(sentiment == "positive"),
    n_neg    = sum(sentiment == "negative"),
    net_per_1000 = (n_pos - n_neg) / n_tokens * 1000,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

party_focus <- article_tokens |>
  filter(category == "politics") |>
  inner_join(party_keywords, by = c("token" = "keyword")) |>
  count(filename, party) |>
  group_by(filename) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), total = sum(n)) |>
  filter(total >= 5, share >= 0.6) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(filename, primary_party = party)

party_sentiment <- article_sent |>
  inner_join(party_focus, by = "filename") |>
  group_by(primary_party) |>
  summarise(n_articles = n(),
            mean_net = mean(net_per_1000) |> round(2)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_net))

# 3) Compose the two panels with patchwork.
library(patchwork)

p_left <- cat_sentiment |>
  ggplot(aes(x = net_per_1000,
             y = fct_reorder(category, net_per_1000),
             fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.1f", net_per_1000)),
            hjust = ifelse(cat_sentiment$net_per_1000 >= 0, -0.15, 1.15),
            size = 3.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "(a) Net sentiment by category",
       x = "Net sentiment (positive - negative) per 1,000 words",
       y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_right <- party_sentiment |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_net,
             y = fct_relevel(primary_party, "Labour", "Conservative", "Lib Dem"),
             fill = primary_party)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.2f  (n=%d)", mean_net, n_articles)),
            hjust = ifelse(party_sentiment$mean_net >= 0, -0.1, 1.1),
            size = 3.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Labour" = "#d62728",
                               "Conservative" = "#1f77b4",
                               "Lib Dem" = "#ff7f0e")) +
  labs(title = "(b) Sentiment of politics articles primarily about each party",
       x = "Net sentiment (positive - negative) per 1,000 words",
       y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_left + p_right + plot_annotation(
  title = "Tone & political balance across the BBC corpus"
)

The two panels tell complementary stories.

Panel (a) – the tone gradient. Entertainment is by far the most upbeat desk (+17.7 net positive words per 1,000), driven by reviews, awards and praise vocabulary. Sport (+8.8) and tech (+5.1) are also positive, but more measured. Business sits exactly at zero (-0.0): the language of profits and sales is balanced almost perfectly by the language of losses, falls and risks. Politics is the only category to come out net-negative (-1.2), which fits a beat dominated by criticism, scandal and opposition-vs-government framing.

Panel (b) – the political balance. Within the 417 politics articles, Labour-related keywords (Labour, Blair, Brown, Blunkett, Prescott) account for 55.9 % of party mentions; the Conservatives (Tories, Howard, Letwin) for 33.3 %; the Liberal Democrats for the remaining 10.8 %. That asymmetry is unsurprising: in 2004-05 Labour was the governing party and naturally generated more news.

The more telling number is the sentiment of articles primarily about each party. After restricting to articles where a party dominates the mentions (>= 60 % of party-keyword references and at least 5 mentions), Labour-focused articles average +2.33 net per 1,000 words and Conservative-focused articles average +1.95 — statistically indistinguishable on a sample of n = 88 vs n = 43. In other words, once the volume difference is controlled for, the BBC’s politics writing is not measurably tilted toward either of the two main parties. The Lib Dem cell is too small to draw conclusions from (n = 5).

5 Interpretation and conclusion

Three findings stand out from the analysis.

The first is that the corpus is well balanced. Each of the five categories contributes between 17 % and 23 % of the total 2,225 articles, so a classifier trained on this corpus does not have to fight a strong class-prior bias.

The second is that the body of the article carries the discriminative signal. Politics and tech pieces are roughly 50 % longer than business or sport pieces, and the per-category vocabulary is sharply distinct (Plot 4). On the other hand, headline length is essentially identical across categories (Plot 3) — a surprising but consistent pattern that reflects house style rather than content.

The third finding goes beyond what each desk writes about and looks at how they write. Categories sit on a clear tone gradient: entertainment articles average +17.7 net-positive words per 1,000, sport +8.8 and tech +5.1; business is exactly neutral (-0.0); politics is the only category to be net-negative (-1.2). That order is intuitive: review-and-award language is upbeat, market language is symmetric (gains and losses cancel), and political coverage skews toward criticism, scandal and opposition framing.

The most striking sub-finding is inside politics itself. Labour dominates the volume of party coverage (55.9 % of party-keyword mentions to the Conservatives’ 33.3 %), but that simply tracks the fact that Labour was the governing party in 2004-05. When we condition on articles that are primarily about a single party, the sentiment is essentially the same on both sides: Labour-focused pieces average +2.33 net per 1,000 words, Conservative-focused pieces +1.95 — a difference well inside the noise of an n = 88 / n = 43 split. So the BBC’s politics writing in this corpus is negative on average, but not detectably tilted toward either of the two main parties. The Lib Dem cell (n = 5) is too small for any inference.

A natural extension would be to compute TF-IDF weights and project the articles into 2-D with irlba::prcomp_irlba plus ggplot2; we would expect to see five well-separated clusters, in line with the lexical fingerprints uncovered above. A second extension would be to swap the Bing lexicon for AFINN [@nielsen2011] or NRC [@mohammad2013]: AFINN adds intensity weights, while NRC adds emotion categories (anger, joy, fear, …) that would let us ask whether politics is just negative or specifically fearful or angry.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(knitr)
library(scales)

# A small helper used throughout the report. It takes any data frame with a
# character column and returns its number of words (whitespace-delimited).
count_words <- function(text) {
  text |>
    stringr::str_squish() |>
    stringr::str_count("\\S+")
}

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

News classification is one of the canonical problems of natural-language
processing: given a piece of text, decide whether it belongs to *business*,
*entertainment*, *politics*, *sport* or *tech*. Long before deep neural
networks made this easy, journalists, librarians and computer scientists
asked a simpler question that still motivates modern systems: **do news
articles in different categories actually look different on the surface?**

This project takes one of the most-cited public benchmarks in the area, the
**BBC News dataset** [@greene2006], and answers that question with a
strictly tidyverse workflow. Concretely, we will:

* describe the structure of the corpus (2,225 articles in five categories);
* derive new features --- length of the title, length of the body, share of
  category-specific vocabulary --- using `mutate`, `filter`, `summarise` and
  `inner_join` chained through the pipe `|>`;
* visualise the resulting patterns with three distinct `ggplot2` charts plus
  a heat-map of the most distinctive words per category;
* draw conclusions about which surface features carry the most discriminative
  power.

The deliverable is a single self-contained Quarto report, intended as a
university-level demonstration of the tidyverse workflow [@wickham2019;
@quarto2024].

# Presentation of the data {#sec-data}

The data was downloaded from Kaggle [@kaggle_bbc] and stored as a single
tab-separated file (`data.csv`). Each row is one news article
collected from the BBC News website between 2004 and 2005.

```{r load-data}
news <- readr::read_tsv("bbc-news-data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(news)
glimpse(news)
```

```{r head-data}
news |>
  head(5) |>
  mutate(content = str_trunc(content, 90)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "First five rows of the raw BBC News data frame.")
```

The data frame contains four columns:

| Column     | Type        | Unit / domain                                                          |
|------------|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `category` | character   | One of `business`, `entertainment`, `politics`, `sport`, `tech`.       |
| `filename` | character   | Original BBC text-file name, e.g. `001.txt`. Identifies the article.   |
| `title`    | character   | Headline of the article (free text, English).                          |
| `content`  | character   | Full body of the article (free text, English, up to ~4,400 words).     |

To enrich the analysis we also load a small auxiliary table that we will
later `inner_join` to the articles. It groups the five categories into
broader newsroom sections.

```{r load-meta}
category_meta <- readr::read_csv("category_meta.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
category_meta |> knitr::kable(caption = "Auxiliary table mapping each category to its broader BBC newsroom section.")
```

# Transformation of data {#sec-transformations}

We now build three derived tables. Each one exercises a different part of
the tidyverse: feature engineering, grouped aggregation and a relational
join.

## Table 1 -- Feature engineering with `mutate` and a user-defined function

We add three new columns: the number of words in the title, the number of
words in the body, and a coarse "long article" flag.

```{r table1}
news_features <- news |>
  mutate(
    title_words   = count_words(title),
    content_words = count_words(content),
    long_article  = if_else(content_words >= 500, "long", "short")
  )

news_features |>
  select(category, filename, title_words, content_words, long_article) |>
  head(8) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Engineered features for the first eight articles.")
```

**Reading the table.** `count_words` is our user-defined helper that uses
`str_squish` (collapses whitespace) and `str_count("\\S+")` (counts
non-whitespace runs). The `long_article` column will let us slice the
corpus by article length later on.

## Table 2 -- Grouped summary with `group_by` + `summarise`

Now we aggregate per category to get a one-row-per-category profile of the
corpus.

```{r table2}
category_summary <- news_features |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    n_articles           = n(),
    avg_title_words      = mean(title_words)   |> round(2),
    avg_content_words    = mean(content_words) |> round(1),
    median_content_words = median(content_words),
    sd_content_words     = sd(content_words)   |> round(1),
    pct_long             = mean(long_article == "long") |> percent(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_articles))

category_summary |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Per-category summary statistics.")
```

**Reading the table.** *Sport* and *business* are the largest categories
(511 and 510 articles); *entertainment* is the smallest (386). Average
article length differs sharply: *politics* and *tech* articles average
~470 and ~440 words respectively, while *business* and *sport* sit closer
to ~330 and ~340. The standard deviations are largest for *politics*
(~300) --- the long-form features push the tail of the distribution far
out.

## Table 3 -- Relational join with `inner_join`

Finally we use `inner_join` to attach the broader-section labels from
`category_meta`, then re-aggregate at the section level.

```{r table3}
section_summary <- news_features |>
  inner_join(category_meta, by = "category") |>
  group_by(broad_section) |>
  summarise(
    n_articles        = n(),
    n_categories      = n_distinct(category),
    avg_content_words = mean(content_words) |> round(1),
    share_long        = mean(content_words >= 500) |> percent(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_articles))

section_summary |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Articles aggregated to the broader newsroom-section level.")
```

**Reading the table.** Once we collapse *business* + *politics* into the
"hard news" section it becomes the largest block of the corpus (927
articles). The "technology" desk has the highest share of long pieces
(~38 %), reflecting feature-style writing about gadgets, software and the
internet. "Sports" remains short and punchy: only ~15 % of articles
reach 500 words.

# Exploratory data analysis {#sec-eda}

## Plot 1 -- Bar chart: corpus composition

```{r plot1, fig.cap="Number of BBC News articles per category."}
news_features |>
  count(category) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(category, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of BBC News articles per category",
    x = "Category", y = "Number of articles"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The five classes are reasonably balanced --- the largest (*sport*, 511) is
only ~32 % bigger than the smallest (*entertainment*, 386). A trained
classifier will not need much resampling; the chart also tells us the
prior probability the BBC editorial team itself assigned to each beat over
the period covered.

## Plot 2 -- Boxplot: how long is the body of an article?

```{r plot2, fig.cap="Distribution of article length (words) by category."}
news_features |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = content_words, fill = category)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.alpha = 0.25, width = 0.55) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of article length (words) by category",
    x = "Category", y = "Words per article"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The boxplot makes clear that *politics* and *tech* are the long-form beats:
the median politics piece is 434 words, almost 50 % longer than the median
business piece (292). *Sport* is the shortest and the most concentrated.
*Entertainment* has a long tail of unusually long features --- profile
pieces of musicians, film reviews, awards round-ups.

## Plot 3 -- Histogram: title length distribution

```{r plot3, fig.cap="Distribution of title word counts by category."}
news_features |>
  ggplot(aes(x = title_words, fill = category)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, position = "identity",
                 alpha = 0.45, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 18)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of title word counts by category",
    x = "Words in title", y = "Count"
  )
```

Headlines, in stark contrast to bodies, are remarkably uniform across
categories: the mode is 5 words for every category, almost no headline
exceeds 12 words, and the densities essentially overlay one another.
Headline length is therefore *not* a useful feature for classification ---
a good reminder that visible style differences sit in the body of the
piece, not in its packaging.

## Plot 4 -- Heatmap: distinctive vocabulary per category

```{r plot4, fig.cap="Distinctive words by category, measured as occurrences per 1,000 words.", fig.height=6}
# A second user-defined helper: turn raw text into a tidy bag-of-words.
tokenise <- function(txt) {
  txt |>
    str_to_lower() |>
    str_extract_all("[a-z]{4,}") |>
    unlist()
}

stop_words <- c("said","also","year","years","first","last","told","more","most",
                "after","before","there","their","they","them","this","that",
                "these","those","with","from","into","about","over","when",
                "what","which","were","been","have","has","had","its","our",
                "are","not","but","you","your","could","would","should",
                "than","then","one","two","very","much","many","such","new")

tokens <- news_features |>
  select(category, content) |>
  mutate(token = map(content, tokenise)) |>
  select(-content) |>
  unnest(token) |>
  filter(!token %in% stop_words)

per_cat_freq <- tokens |>
  group_by(category, token) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(category) |>
  mutate(per_1000 = n / sum(n) * 1000) |>
  ungroup()

# Keep words that are highly concentrated in a single category.
global_freq <- per_cat_freq |>
  group_by(token) |>
  summarise(global_per_1000 = sum(n) / sum(per_cat_freq$n) * 1000)

distinctive <- per_cat_freq |>
  inner_join(global_freq, by = "token") |>
  mutate(lift = per_1000 / global_per_1000) |>
  filter(n >= 60, lift >= 2) |>           # frequent in this category and disproportionately so
  group_by(category) |>
  slice_max(per_1000, n = 7, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

distinctive |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = fct_reorder(token, per_1000), fill = per_1000)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(per_1000, 1)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distinctive words by category (per 1,000 words)",
    x = "Category", y = NULL, fill = "per 1,000 words"
  )
```

This is the most informative visualisation in the report. The bright
diagonal blocks tell us the model's job will be relatively easy:

* *Business* is dominated by **market, company, growth, firm, economy, bank, sales**.
* *Entertainment* is dominated by **film, best, music, show, awards, award, star**.
* *Politics* is dominated by **labour, government, party, election, blair, minister, brown**.
* *Sport* is dominated by **game, against, england, players, team, play**.
* *Tech* is dominated by **technology, mobile, users, games, software, digital, computer**.

Crucially, almost no word from one category appears in the top-7
distinctive list of another category. This is empirical confirmation that
**lexical features alone** carry most of the classification signal in this
dataset --- which is why simple TF-IDF + linear SVM models routinely score
above 95 % accuracy on it.

## Plot 5 -- Tone and political balance: sentiment per category, plus a Labour-vs-Conservative deep-dive

Beyond *what* each desk writes about, we can also ask about *tone*: are
some categories systematically more positive than others, and within
politics is the BBC's coverage of the major UK parties tilted in any
direction? We use the **Bing opinion lexicon** [@hu2004], available out of
the box via `tidytext::get_sentiments("bing")`.

```{r plot5, fig.cap="Net sentiment per category (a) and Labour-vs-Conservative breakdown within politics (b).", fig.width=11, fig.height=4.6}
library(tidytext)

# 1) Per-category sentiment: tokenise every article, join the Bing
#    lexicon, summarise to a single number per category.
bing <- tidytext::get_sentiments("bing")

article_tokens <- news_features |>
  select(category, filename, content) |>
  mutate(token = map(content, tokenise)) |>
  select(-content) |>
  unnest(token)

cat_sentiment <- article_tokens |>
  inner_join(bing, by = c("token" = "word")) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    n_tokens = n(),
    n_pos    = sum(sentiment == "positive"),
    n_neg    = sum(sentiment == "negative"),
    net_per_1000 = (n_pos - n_neg) / n_tokens * 1000
  ) |>
  arrange(net_per_1000)

# 2) Politics deep-dive: build party-keyword bags, classify each politics
#    article by the party that dominates its mentions, and average the
#    article-level sentiment per party.
party_keywords <- tribble(
  ~party,         ~keyword,
  "Labour",       "labour",
  "Labour",       "blair",
  "Labour",       "brown",
  "Labour",       "blunkett",
  "Labour",       "prescott",
  "Conservative", "tory",
  "Conservative", "tories",
  "Conservative", "conservative",
  "Conservative", "howard",
  "Conservative", "letwin",
  "Lib Dem",      "kennedy",
  "Lib Dem",      "libdem",
  "Lib Dem",      "campbell"
)

article_sent <- article_tokens |>
  inner_join(bing, by = c("token" = "word")) |>
  group_by(category, filename) |>
  summarise(
    n_tokens = n(),
    n_pos    = sum(sentiment == "positive"),
    n_neg    = sum(sentiment == "negative"),
    net_per_1000 = (n_pos - n_neg) / n_tokens * 1000,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

party_focus <- article_tokens |>
  filter(category == "politics") |>
  inner_join(party_keywords, by = c("token" = "keyword")) |>
  count(filename, party) |>
  group_by(filename) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), total = sum(n)) |>
  filter(total >= 5, share >= 0.6) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(filename, primary_party = party)

party_sentiment <- article_sent |>
  inner_join(party_focus, by = "filename") |>
  group_by(primary_party) |>
  summarise(n_articles = n(),
            mean_net = mean(net_per_1000) |> round(2)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_net))

# 3) Compose the two panels with patchwork.
library(patchwork)

p_left <- cat_sentiment |>
  ggplot(aes(x = net_per_1000,
             y = fct_reorder(category, net_per_1000),
             fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.1f", net_per_1000)),
            hjust = ifelse(cat_sentiment$net_per_1000 >= 0, -0.15, 1.15),
            size = 3.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "(a) Net sentiment by category",
       x = "Net sentiment (positive - negative) per 1,000 words",
       y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_right <- party_sentiment |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_net,
             y = fct_relevel(primary_party, "Labour", "Conservative", "Lib Dem"),
             fill = primary_party)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.2f  (n=%d)", mean_net, n_articles)),
            hjust = ifelse(party_sentiment$mean_net >= 0, -0.1, 1.1),
            size = 3.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Labour" = "#d62728",
                               "Conservative" = "#1f77b4",
                               "Lib Dem" = "#ff7f0e")) +
  labs(title = "(b) Sentiment of politics articles primarily about each party",
       x = "Net sentiment (positive - negative) per 1,000 words",
       y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_left + p_right + plot_annotation(
  title = "Tone & political balance across the BBC corpus"
)
```

The two panels tell complementary stories.

**Panel (a) -- the tone gradient.** Entertainment is by far the most
upbeat desk (+17.7 net positive words per 1,000), driven by reviews,
awards and praise vocabulary. Sport (+8.8) and tech (+5.1) are also
positive, but more measured. Business sits exactly at zero (-0.0): the
language of profits and sales is balanced almost perfectly by the language
of losses, falls and risks. Politics is the **only** category to come out
net-negative (-1.2), which fits a beat dominated by criticism, scandal and
opposition-vs-government framing.

**Panel (b) -- the political balance.** Within the 417 politics articles,
Labour-related keywords (Labour, Blair, Brown, Blunkett, Prescott) account
for **55.9 %** of party mentions; the Conservatives (Tories, Howard,
Letwin) for **33.3 %**; the Liberal Democrats for the remaining 10.8 %.
That asymmetry is unsurprising: in 2004-05 Labour was the governing party
and naturally generated more news.

The more telling number is the *sentiment* of articles primarily about
each party. After restricting to articles where a party dominates the
mentions (>= 60 % of party-keyword references and at least 5 mentions),
**Labour-focused articles average +2.33 net per 1,000 words and
Conservative-focused articles average +1.95** --- statistically
indistinguishable on a sample of n = 88 vs n = 43. In other words, once
the volume difference is controlled for, the BBC's politics writing is
**not measurably tilted toward either of the two main parties**. The Lib
Dem cell is too small to draw conclusions from (n = 5).

# Interpretation and conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

Three findings stand out from the analysis.

The first is that **the corpus is well balanced**. Each of the five
categories contributes between 17 % and 23 % of the total 2,225 articles,
so a classifier trained on this corpus does not have to fight a strong
class-prior bias.

The second is that **the body of the article carries the discriminative
signal**. Politics and tech pieces are roughly 50 % longer than business
or sport pieces, and the per-category vocabulary is sharply distinct
(Plot 4). On the other hand, **headline length is essentially identical
across categories** (Plot 3) --- a surprising but consistent pattern that
reflects house style rather than content.

The third finding goes beyond *what* each desk writes about and looks at
*how* they write. Categories sit on a clear tone gradient: entertainment
articles average **+17.7** net-positive words per 1,000, sport **+8.8**
and tech **+5.1**; business is exactly neutral (**-0.0**); politics is the
only category to be net-negative (**-1.2**). That order is intuitive:
review-and-award language is upbeat, market language is symmetric (gains
and losses cancel), and political coverage skews toward criticism,
scandal and opposition framing.

The most striking sub-finding is **inside politics itself**. Labour
dominates the *volume* of party coverage (**55.9 %** of party-keyword
mentions to the Conservatives' 33.3 %), but that simply tracks the fact
that Labour was the governing party in 2004-05. When we condition on
articles that are primarily *about* a single party, the sentiment is
essentially the same on both sides: Labour-focused pieces average
**+2.33** net per 1,000 words, Conservative-focused pieces **+1.95** ---
a difference well inside the noise of an n = 88 / n = 43 split. So the
BBC's politics writing in this corpus is *negative on average*, but not
detectably tilted toward either of the two main parties. The Lib Dem
cell (n = 5) is too small for any inference.

A natural extension would be to compute TF-IDF weights and project the
articles into 2-D with `irlba::prcomp_irlba` plus `ggplot2`; we would
expect to see five well-separated clusters, in line with the lexical
fingerprints uncovered above. A second extension would be to swap the
Bing lexicon for **AFINN** [@nielsen2011] or **NRC** [@mohammad2013]: AFINN
adds intensity weights, while NRC adds emotion categories (anger, joy,
fear, ...) that would let us ask whether politics is just *negative* or
specifically *fearful* or *angry*.
